title: After 1997, 175 south-east Australian catchments lost a share of flow that grew in wet years, unlike any one-parameter Budyko change; the eastern US form was unresolved (annual, 1951-2025)
abstract: Question: after 1997, runoff in south-east Australia (SE-AU) and the eastern US (East-US) fell below the 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation. Earlier work reported a slope loss in SE-AU and a constant offset in East-US. Do the two forms show two causes, or only different positions on the aridity curve? Approach: 175 SE-AU and 260 East-US CAMELS catchments (annual flow, AGCD/SILO and nClimGrid rain). For each catchment we fitted a Budyko (Fu) form curve on 1951-1996. Then we fitted seven one-parameter mechanisms to the test years: constant loss, proportional loss, effective-rain loss, rain scaling, energy-limit change, Budyko-partition change and wet-year-excess loss. We used cell-bootstrap intervals, a 1981-1996 placebo, and synthetic shape ratios k = slope change / offset. Results: on a Budyko curve, no single-parameter change of climate or partition gives k above about 1. In SE-AU (2010-2021) the proportional loss (median 21.6% of flow) was best and all other mechanisms were rejected, including the partition change. But k was 1.57 (95% CI 1.13-2.19), and 1.86-1.95 with linear and quadratic calibrations: the loss grew faster than flow in wet years. The SE-AU slope loss (-0.20 to -0.26) occurred at all runoff ratios. At equal runoff ratio it exceeded East-US by 0.14 (0.07-0.20). Rain-noise attenuation explains at most 4%. East-US lost about 7% at mean rain (38.8 mm/yr against 41.5 mm/yr in SE-AU), but its form depended on the calibration: k = 0.89 (Fu) against 0.04 (linear), and cross-validation did not choose between them. Conclusion: the SE-AU change is regional, is not a simple Budyko-curve change, and removes extra flow in wet years. The East-US offset form is not robust. Limitations: annual fingerprints do not identify processes; several tests are post hoc; SE-AU flow ends in 2021.

display.caption: Flow residual in 2010-end against the annual rain anomaly, as a percentage of mean 1951-1996 flow, with the residual that each fitted mechanism predicts. SE-AU loses little in dry years and much in wet years, between a proportional loss (M2) and a wet-year excess loss (M7). East-US cannot separate M1, M2 and M6.

Mean normalised error of each one-parameter mechanism minus the best one, with 95% cell-bootstrap intervals, for 2010-end and for the 1981-1996 placebo. The proportional loss is best in SE-AU (AGCD and SILO) and East-US. In SE-AU all other mechanisms are rejected with AGCD rain.

Left: rain-slope change by runoff-ratio class. SE-AU loses 20-26% at all runoff ratios; East-US loses 4-8% at the same runoff ratios. Right: theoretical shape ratio k for each mechanism on a Fu curve, and observed k with three calibration forms. SE-AU k is above 1 with all forms; East-US k depends on the form.

citations.reason: We reuse its annual CAMELS-AUS and US flow and rain tables and catchment rules. We confirm its SE-AU slope loss with a cross-validated Budyko-form calibration, and we show that its constant-offset form for East-US depends on the linear calibration.
We reuse its nClimGrid basin water-year rain and temperature table.
It found about 40 mm/yr losses in both regions after 2009; we find 41.5 and 38.8 mm/yr, and we show that the regional difference in slope loss remains at equal runoff ratio.
Its effective-rainfall fingerprint for flow components; we test effective-rain loss and six other fingerprints in the annual rain dimension.
Regional southern Australian change after 1997; our runoff-ratio analysis also shows that the change is regional.
First report of the post-1997 shifts in both regions.
Victorian low-runoff state through wet years; our wet-year excess loss gives one explanation of its persistence.
Seasonal rainfall fits at Victorian gauges; seasonal rain is not in our annual model.
